title: General claim, then the detail (For example vs Specifically / In particular)
subtitle: Transitions · 25 official questions

sections.heading: Where this sits for you
body: **25 of the official questions in Transitions are this one** — 8 Easy, 14 Medium, 3 Hard.
It is bottom-heavy, which makes it cheap points. Secure it early.

sections.heading: How to spot it
body: You are looking at this pattern when:
- Sentence one makes a broad claim: 'several roles', 'improved upon', 'has also done', 'underwent a transformation', 'many authors'.
- Choices often include both 'for example' and 'specifically' or 'in particular', or one of them next to contrast and sequence decoys.

sections.heading: The method
body: - 1) Confirm that sentence two is narrower than sentence one and agrees with it.
- 2) Decide whether it's one instance out of several possible ones ('for example') or an exact spelling-out of the same claim ('specifically', 'in particular').
- If sentence one mentions a single vague thing and sentence two says exactly what it was, pick 'specifically'.
- If sentence one mentions a class or a plural and sentence two picks one member, pick 'for example'.
- 3) Eliminate anything that implies contrast or time order.

sections.heading: What it is built to catch
body: You choose 'for example' when sentence one names one single event or action and sentence two just restates it in detail.
Nothing is being chosen from a set, so 'specifically' is the answer.
The reverse mistake also happens: you pick 'in other words' when sentence two adds new, narrower information and doesn't simply rephrase.

sections.heading: You are losing these
body: Before you choose, say out loud what the question is asking for — not what you solved for.
You choose 'for example' when sentence one names one single event or action and sentence two just restates it in detail.
Nothing is being chosen from a set, so 'specifically' is the answer.
